opus-5.5.text:
Well, the basic problem was that the frontier of human knowledge is really spread out. No single person, or even a small team, can write questions that sit at the edge of expertise across mathematics, classics, ecology, chemistry, linguistics, and so on. If you want a benchmark that's actually hard for these models, you need the people who are deep in each of those niches. So it made sense to make it a broad, global call and let thousands of specialists each contribute what they know best.

Asking each person for a few questions rather than dozens was partly practical. These are busy researchers and professors. Writing one really good question, one that's unambiguous, has a verifiable answer, and that frontier models get wrong, takes real effort. It's much easier to get high-quality contributions if you're asking for a small slice of someone's time. It also gives you diversity. You get breadth across subfields instead of a few people's particular tastes dominating the dataset.

There was also a filtering step built into it. We'd run candidate questions against the leading models, and if the models could already answer them, those questions didn't make the cut. Then there was human review on top of that. So the crowd-sourcing wasn't just about volume. It was about collecting a large pool of expert-level material and then distilling it down to the things that were genuinely beyond current systems.

The deeper motivation is that benchmarks have been saturating really quickly. MMLU and similar tests went from hard to basically solved in a couple of years. We wanted something closer to the ceiling of closed-ended, academic knowledge, so that when models do start doing well on it, that tells you something meaningful. Getting there required pulling in expertise from all over the world.

r001.rationale: The response says existing benchmarks had gone from hard to basically solved, motivating a higher-ceiling benchmark whose results would be meaningful.

r002.rationale: It explains that no individual or small team could cover the frontier across many fields, and that specialists could contribute a few questions each.

r003.rationale: It describes a benchmark near the ceiling of closed-ended academic knowledge, with questions that have verifiable answers, but does not clearly identify reasoning as part of the human frontier being approximated.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the basic observation was that the existing benchmarks were saturating. MMLU, GPQA, things like that—models went from essentially random to near ceiling in a couple of years, and once you're at ninety-plus percent the benchmark stops telling you anything. So we wanted something that would actually be at the frontier of human knowledge, where the questions are hard not because they're tricky or adversarial in a gimmicky way, but because they're genuinely at the edge of what a specialist in that field knows.

And the thing is, no single person, no single lab, can write that. I can't write a frontier question in Byzantine history or in organic chemistry or in some corner of category theory. The only people who can write a question that's genuinely difficult for a PhD in field X are people who are themselves at that level in field X. So the structure of the problem basically forces you into a distributed approach. You need thousands of people, each contributing a few questions from their own area, because expertise is spread thinly across the world and no one has very much of it in aggregate.

There's a second reason, which is coverage. If you have a small team writing questions, you get the biases of that team—they'll overrepresent math and computer science because that's what they know. Having contributors across a hundred-plus countries and many dozens of disciplines gives you something that's closer to a sample of human knowledge rather than a sample of what Bay Area researchers find interesting.

And then from a contamination standpoint, having lots of people each write a handful of original questions is actually a nice property. These questions have never appeared on the internet, they're not pulled from textbooks or problem sets, so you're not just measuring whether the model memorized the answer somewhere in pretraining.

We also did a filtering pass where we ran the submissions against frontier models and only kept the ones the models got wrong, and then had expert review on top of that. So it's a bit of a funnel—many thousands of submissions down to a few thousand questions. The incentive design mattered too; we had a prize pool and coauthorship for contributors, which is a cheap way to get a very large number of highly qualified people to spend an afternoon on it.

The name is a little tongue-in-cheek, but the idea is serious: this is meant to be roughly the last closed-ended academic benchmark of this type, because once models are doing well on this, there isn't much further to go with the "test the model on questions humans know the answer to" paradigm. After that, you have to move to things like open-ended research, or actual real-world task performance, where the evaluation itself is much harder.

r001.rationale: The response says existing benchmarks reached near-ceiling scores and then stopped telling us much, making further capability gains hard to see.

r002.rationale: It says no individual or lab can write frontier questions across fields, so thousands of specialists each contribute a few from their area.

r003.rationale: It describes a benchmark at the frontier of human knowledge and a closed-ended test using questions with known answers, but does not characterize it as measuring the frontier of reasoning.

astra-6.text:
The idea was to get enough breadth and depth that the benchmark wouldn’t just reflect what a small group of people happens to know. If you want questions at the frontier of human expertise, you need people from many different disciplines contributing within their own specialties.

And asking for just a few questions makes it easier for experts to participate while focusing on quality. Someone might not have time to build an entire benchmark, but they can contribute a question that requires a really deep understanding of their field. Bringing those contributions together lets us test a much wider range of capabilities than we could develop ourselves.

r001.rationale: It discusses breadth and expert participation, but does not say existing AI evaluations had saturated or that this made capability advances harder to discern.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the difficulty of building an entire benchmark with the easier contribution of a single deep question, capturing the individual-expert-versus-few-questions mismatch.

r003.rationale: It says the benchmark tests a wider range of capabilities, but does not characterize it as an approximation of the human frontier of knowledge and reasoning for closed-ended questions with known answers.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic problem is that it’s very hard for any one person, or even one team, to write a large number of questions at the frontier of human knowledge. An expert might have a few really good questions in their specialty—questions that are difficult, have a clear answer, and require substantial expertise. But asking them to write hundreds would be a very different proposition.

So we wanted to spread that effort across a broad range of experts around the world. If each person contributes just a few of their best questions, you can assemble something much more challenging and diverse than a small team could produce on its own. You also reduce the extent to which the benchmark reflects one group’s particular strengths or interests.

The goal was to get a clearer picture of where models still fall short across many areas of expertise, rather than just making another test that they would quickly saturate.

r001.rationale: It mentions avoiding another test that models would quickly saturate, but does not explain that saturation of existing evaluations made AI capability progress difficult to discern.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the difficulty of one person or team writing many frontier-level questions with experts contributing a few strong questions each.

r003.rationale: It describes difficult questions with clear answers across many expertise areas, but does not characterize the exam as an approximation of the human frontier of knowledge and reasoning for closed-ended questions with known answers.
